extracted.intended_audience: maritime historians, sailing enthusiasts, and students of merchant sailing performance
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and measures used in the text to judge the performance, seaworthiness and commercial success of late-19th / early-20th century sailing ships (clipper/four-mast barques) on long passages to/from Australia and other ports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage duration (total days out)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total elapsed days for a voyage (examples: 'passage worked out at 69 days pilot to pilot, 73 days port to port'; tables of 'PASSAGES TO SYDNEY UNDER 80 DAYS', 'PASSAGES TO MELBOURNE UNDER 80 DAYS').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly records and compares voyages by 'days out' (departure-to-arrival). Records and notable passages are highlighted when under benchmark thresholds (notably 80 days). Tables list departure, key waypoints and arrival dates to compute days out.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24‑hour run (miles per day)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance run in a single 24‑hour period (e.g. 'she ran 300 miles in the 24 hours', 'best 24 hours 327 miles', 'best run in the 24 hours was 345 miles').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a short-term performance metric; consecutive 24‑hour runs are often cited to show sustained speed (examples: series like 303, 290, 288, ... miles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best week's work (weekly miles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total miles run over a seven‑day period (e.g. 'Her best week’s work was 2119 knots' and other weekly totals such as 1698, 1798, 1908, 1929 miles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly aggregates demonstrate sustained high performance beyond single-day bursts; presented alongside 24‑hour runs to characterise form during easting-down or trade-wind stretches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Route selection and waypoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of navigational route (e.g., via south of New Zealand, rounding the Snares, Bass Strait, via Tasmania, crossing Cape meridian) and its effect on passage time ('skippers generally preferring the shorter route through Bass Straits', 'it would have been hard lines if I could not have rounded the Snares in 14 days').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative attributes significant differences in voyage duration to chosen routings and positions when rounding key waypoints; route choice is a deliberate performance factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather and wind conditions encountered
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevailing winds, gales, calms, fog, squalls and swell that affected progress (examples: 'lost S.E. trades', 'had strong head winds', 'unusually heavy gale with a tremendous cross sea', 'gentle S.W. breeze', 'foggy; ice ahead').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance is consistently contextualised by wind and weather reports; accounts note when fast runs occurred under favourable trades or when passages were slowed by headwinds, calms or storms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encounter with ice and ice‑hazard handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of encountering field ice and huge icebergs, and the ship’s navigation/handling through ice ('encountered ice 1000 feet high', 'a whole horizon to windward was a complete mass of bergs', 'tacked ship... to keep clear of huge pieces').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed first‑hand accounts describe lookout use, tacking, reducing speed, selecting channels, and close-quarters passage between bergs; used to evaluate seamanship and survivability in southern latitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hull condition / fouled bottom
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of hull fouling on speed and passage quality ('owing to the foulness of her bottom his ship was not sailing her best', 'her bottom was probably foul').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fouled bottom is explicitly cited as a cause for poor passages and reduced day/weekly runs; maintenance state is therefore a performance criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cargo load and stowage (deadweight/draught)
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence of cargo amount and distribution on sailing performance ('had between 4000 and 5000 tons of heavy general cargo in her hold and was very deep', 'this performance... is equal to any of that day' despite heavy load).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deeply laden ships are noted as slower or more difficult to handle; exceptional performances while heavily loaded are flagged as notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design, build quality and technological innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ship design and fittings that affect performance and durability (e.g., Port Jackson 'designed by Mr. Alexander Duthie', Derwent innovations: 'one of the first ships to cross steel topgallant yards, substitute rigging screws for deadeyes, to have a donkey with winch barrels').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific design choices and innovations are cited as reasons for speed, strength and handling characteristics; design pedigree is used to judge a ship’s potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seamanship and storm management techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Captain and crew tactics to survive storms and heavy seas (examples: 'Captain Pattman using oil with good effect', 'reduced speed', 'stood on', 'squared away').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical seamanship measures (using oil, reducing or increasing sail, tactical tacks) are invoked to explain successful outcomes in gales and heavy cross seas; effectiveness of officers is an implicit evaluation point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew quality, discipline and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Competence, discipline and availability of crew and officers (examples: crew refused duty on Derwent; 'lack of real sailormen to man her' forcing captain to give up command; issues hiring men in San Francisco at extortionate rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human factors—experienced certificated officers, capable hands, and crew discipline—are repeatedly tied to safe and fast passages; crew shortages and poor crew quality are blamed for degraded performance or command changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative performance / races and records
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging ships by head‑to‑head races or comparison with contemporaries and steamers (e.g., race to Valparaiso with Wendur, comparison to mail steamer Aberdeen, many tables comparing ships under 80 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Races and ranking tables are used as a normative framework: a ship’s reputation is determined by where it sits in these comparisons and whether it sets or equals records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural damage, losses and repair impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage sustained (boats, half-deck burst in, decks swept off, stove broken) and subsequent repair bills that affect future voyages ('decks were badly swept off the Horn and she had a big repair bill', 'had to dock...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents that cause structural damage are recorded and linked to slower subsequent passages, increased costs and changes in commercial viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling characteristics and stability (tenderness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic handling traits such as being 'tender' or 'ticklish to handle' and practices adopted ('though a very fast ship, was also a ticklish ship to handle, being rather tender, and Captain Clarke always sent down royal yards when in port').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traits inform operational procedures (e.g., reducing sail in port) and are part of a qualitative judgment about a ship’s suitability for certain trades or commanders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health, passengers' condition and quarantine implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Voyage health issues (e.g., 'arrived with 414 emigrants, and had measles and fever on board so had to go into quarantine').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disease outbreaks among passengers are noted as operational events that can delay arrival, require quarantine, and affect a ship’s commercial and reputational standing.
